title: Sample Efficient Generative Molecular Optimization with Joint Self-Improvement
claim: A joint generative-predictive model trained on offline data iteratively steers generation toward high-scoring outputs at inference time.
layout: 4 stages, left-to-right, tree diagrams showing before/after probability biasing

caption: Overview of JSI. In the offline setting, a joint generative-predictive model, with a language modeling (LM) head for next-token probability prediction and a predictive head for property prediction, is fine-tuned on an offline dataset of molecules and their property scores, and the model self-improves by iteratively biasing next-token probabilities (blue) using predicted property scores (green), steering generation towards high-scoring molecules at inference time. In the online setting, ground-truth oracle evaluations are used in place of the predictive head.
abstract: Generative molecular optimization aims to design molecules with properties surpassing those of existing compounds. However, evaluating candidate molecules is expensive, so sample efficiency, i.e., generating optimized molecules within a fixed evaluation budget, is essential. Moreover, in the offline setting, where a surrogate model approximates candidate evaluation, sample inefficiency compounds with surrogate error, further limiting performance. To address these challenges, we introduce Joint Self-Improvement (JSI), a framework for sample-efficient online and offline molecular optimization. JSI combines (i) a joint generative-predictive model trained via a joint likelihood-based loss, which aligns molecule generation and surrogate modeling, and (ii) inference-time self-improvement, which iteratively biases the generative component of the joint model toward higher-scoring molecules, using direct objective function evaluations in the online setting and the predictive component in the offline setting. Experiments across docking score optimization in both online and offline settings, as well as antimicrobial peptide optimization, demonstrate that JSI outperforms state-of-the-art methods under limited evaluation budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/szczurek-lab/jsi.
